learn.b: A business makes goods, like shoes, or provides services, like haircuts, to earn money. It exists to meet customer needs. Some businesses sell both.
Revenue is the money from sales. Expenses are the costs of running the business. Profit is revenue minus expenses.
Stakeholders are people affected by a business: owners, employees, customers, suppliers and the community. Good businesses think about all of them.

qs.q: What is revenue?
qs.why: Revenue is the total sales income.

qs.q: How is profit calculated?
qs.why: Profit is what remains after expenses.

qs.q: Which is a service?
qs.why: Services are actions done for customers, not physical items.

qs.q: Who is a stakeholder of a business?
qs.why: Employees, customers, suppliers and owners are all affected.

qs.q: A business always makes a profit.
qs.why: If expenses exceed revenue, a business has a loss.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of running a lemonade stand in order

lab.q: Challenge: A bakery has revenue of $1,200 and expenses of $850. What is the profit in dollars?
Challenge: A shop sells 40 cakes at $15 each. What is the revenue in dollars?
lab.hint: Multiply the number sold by the price.

lab.q: Challenge: People affected by a business, like owners, employees and customers, are called what?
lab.why: They are stakeholders because the business affects them.

learn.b: A sole proprietorship has one owner who keeps all profit and is personally responsible for debts. A partnership has two or more owners who share profit and responsibility.
An LLC, limited liability company, is a flexible structure. In general it keeps owners' personal belongings separate from business debts. This is called limited liability.
A corporation is a separate legal entity owned by shareholders. It can raise money by selling shares. It is more complex and has more rules.

qs.q: How many owners does a sole proprietorship have?
qs.why: Sole means one owner.

qs.q: What does limited liability mean?
o: Owners are generally not personally responsible for all business debts
qs.why: Personal assets are generally protected from business debts.

qs.q: What is a corporation?
o: A separate legal entity owned by shareholders
qs.why: A corporation is legally separate from its owners.

qs.q: How many owners does a partnership have?
qs.why: Partnerships are owned by two or more people.

qs.q: An LLC can generally protect owners' personal assets from business debts.
qs.why: Limited liability is the main feature of an LLC.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of forming a company in order

lab.q: Challenge: Which structure has one owner who is personally responsible for the debts? (two words)
lab.hint: One owner, no separate legal entity.
lab.why: A sole proprietorship has no legal separation between owner and business.

lab.q: Challenge: What does LLC stand for?
lab.hint: The middle word is the key idea: owners' belongings are protected.

lab.q: Challenge: The owners of a corporation are called what?
lab.why: Shareholders own parts of the corporation through shares.

learn.b: Demand is how much buyers want at a price. When the price goes up, buyers usually want less. Supply is how much sellers offer. When the price goes up, sellers usually offer more.
The equilibrium price is where the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded. If the price is too low, there is a shortage. If it is too high, there is a surplus, so goods are left unsold.
Scarcity means resources are limited but wants are not. Opportunity cost is the next best choice you give up. A monopoly has one seller. Competition between many sellers usually keeps prices fair.

qs.q: When the price of a product goes up, what usually happens to the quantity buyers want?
qs.why: Higher prices usually reduce the quantity demanded.

qs.q: A shortage happens when:
o: Quantity supplied is higher than demanded
Quantity demanded is higher than quantity supplied
qs.why: Buyers want more than sellers offer, so the product runs out.

qs.q: What is the equilibrium price?
o: The price where supply equals demand
The price set by the government
The price of the best seller
qs.why: At equilibrium, buyers and sellers agree on quantity.

qs.q: What is opportunity cost?
o: The cost of making a product
The value of the next best choice you give up
qs.why: Choosing one thing means giving up the next best option.

qs.q: A market with only one seller is called a monopoly.
qs.why: Mono means one: one seller controls the market.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Many sellers try to win buyers

qs.q: Put these steps in order when a price is set too low
items: The price is set too low

lab.q: Challenge: One company is the only seller in a market. What is this called?
lab.why: A single seller is a monopoly.

lab.q: Challenge: You pay $20 for a game instead of a $20 fan. What do we call the value of the fan you gave up?
lab.hint: Two words: it is the cost of the next best choice.
lab.why: The fan is the opportunity cost of buying the game.

lab.q: Challenge: At $5 buyers want 120 sunglasses but sellers offer only 80. How many sunglasses is the shortage?

learn.b: A supply chain is the path from raw materials to the customer. Inventory is the goods a business holds for sale. Too little means lost sales, too much ties up money.
Managers plan (set goals), organize (arrange people and resources), lead (guide and motivate) and control (check results and fix problems).
SWOT stands for Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats. Strengths and weaknesses are inside the business. Opportunities and threats come from outside, like new rivals.

qs.q: What is a supply chain?
o: The path from raw materials to the customer
qs.why: It covers everything needed to get a product to buyers.

qs.q: What is inventory?
o: Goods a business holds for sale
qs.why: Inventory is the stock of goods ready to sell.

qs.q: What does the T in SWOT stand for?
qs.why: SWOT is Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats.

qs.q: Which management function means setting goals and deciding how to reach them?
qs.why: Planning sets the goals and the path.

qs.q: Opportunities and threats in a SWOT analysis are internal to the company.
qs.why: They are external; strengths and weaknesses are internal.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the management functions in order

lab.q: Challenge: In SWOT, what does the S stand for?
lab.hint: It is something good inside the business.
lab.why: SWOT is Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats.

lab.q: Challenge: Which management function means setting goals and deciding how to reach them?
lab.hint: It comes first: plan, organize, lead, control.
lab.why: Planning sets the goals and the path to them.

lab.q: Challenge: put the supply chain in order
lab.why: A supply chain runs from raw materials to the customer.

learn.b: Human resources (HR) finds and supports employees. Hiring usually goes: write a job description, advertise, interview, make an offer, then train. Training helps new workers do the job well.
A wage is pay by the hour. A salary is a fixed amount per year. Benefits are extras such as health insurance and paid time off. Turnover is how often employees leave and must be replaced.

People work best with clear goals, good communication and recognition, not only money. Laws set rules such as minimum wage and safe workplaces. It is illegal to refuse a job because of someone's race or religion.

qs.q: What is a salary?
o: Pay only for each hour worked
A fixed amount paid per year
qs.why: A salary stays the same regardless of the exact hours.

qs.q: Which of these is an employee benefit?
qs.why: Benefits are extras given on top of pay.

qs.q: What is usually the first step in hiring?
qs.why: You must know what the job needs before you search.

qs.q: Which is illegal when hiring in most countries?
o: Rejecting someone because of their religion
qs.why: Discrimination is against the law.

qs.q: Employees are motivated only by money.
qs.why: Recognition, goals and growth also motivate people.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the hiring steps in order

lab.q: Challenge: An employee earns $12 per hour and works 30 hours. What is the pay in dollars?
Challenge: A salary is $24,000 per year, paid in 12 equal months. What is one monthly payment in dollars?
Challenge: When employees leave and must be replaced, the rate is called employee what?
lab.why: Turnover measures how often workers leave.

learn.b: Cash flow is the movement of money in and out of a business. Positive cash flow means more comes in than goes out. A profitable business can still run out of cash if customers pay late.
The break-even point is when revenue equals total costs, so profit is zero. Economies of scale mean the cost per unit falls as a business makes more.
Products go through introduction, growth, maturity and decline. Business ethics means doing the right thing, such as honest ads and fair pay. Trust helps a business last.

qs.q: What is cash flow?
o: Movement of money in and out
qs.why: Cash flow tracks money entering and leaving.

qs.q: What are economies of scale?
o: Cost per unit falls as output grows
qs.why: Making more can spread costs and lower the unit cost.

qs.q: What is the break-even point?
qs.why: At break-even, profit is zero.

qs.q: Which is the first stage of the product life cycle?
qs.why: A product starts with its introduction to the market.

qs.q: A profitable business can still run out of cash.
qs.why: Timing matters: if money arrives late, bills may go unpaid.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Lower unit cost with more output

qs.q: Put the product life cycle in order

lab.q: Challenge: Fixed costs are $500 and each unit adds $5 after variable costs. How many units are needed to break even?
lab.hint: Divide fixed costs by the amount each unit adds.

lab.q: Challenge: A business takes in $900 and pays out $650 in a month. What is the net cash flow in dollars?
Challenge: Which stage of the product life cycle comes right after growth?
lab.why: After growth, sales level off in maturity.

learn.b: Laws are rules you must follow. Ethics is about what is right. Something can be legal but still unethical, like misleading customers in a way the law does not cover.

CSR, corporate social responsibility, means a business cares about society and the environment, not only profit. Examples are cutting waste, fair pay and donating. Sustainability means meeting today's needs without harming the future.

Bribery is paying to get unfair favors. Fraud is lying to gain money unfairly. A conflict of interest is when personal gain clashes with your duty. A whistleblower reports wrongdoing inside an organization.

qs.q: What does CSR stand for?
qs.why: CSR is about a company's duty to society.

qs.q: A company legally dumps waste that harms a river. How is this best described?
qs.why: Following the law does not make an action right.

qs.q: What does the triple bottom line measure?
qs.why: It adds social and environmental results to profit.

qs.q: What is a whistleblower?
o: Someone who reports wrongdoing inside an organization
qs.why: Whistleblowers expose wrongdoing.

qs.q: If something is legal, it is always ethical.
qs.why: Some legal actions are still unfair or harmful.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Meeting needs without harming the future

qs.q: Put these steps in order after a company finds an unsafe product

lab.q: Challenge: What do we call a person who reports wrongdoing inside an organization?
lab.hint: One word, it involves blowing a whistle.

lab.q: Challenge: The triple bottom line is people, planet and what?
lab.hint: It is the traditional business goal.
lab.why: The three Ps are people, planet and profit.

lab.q: Challenge: Paying someone money to get an unfair favor is called what?

learn.b: An import is a good bought from another country. An export is a good sold to another country. Trade lets countries focus on what they make best.
A tariff is a tax on imported goods. A quota limits how much of a good can be imported. Both can protect local businesses but raise prices for buyers.

An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. If $1 = 0.90 euros, then $100 = 90 euros. Outsourcing is paying another company, often abroad, to do some work. A multinational operates in many countries.

qs.q: What is an export?
o: A good sold to another country
A good bought from another country
qs.why: Exports leave the country to be sold abroad.

qs.q: What is a tariff?
qs.why: Tariffs make imports more expensive.

qs.q: If $1 equals 0.90 euros, how many euros is $50?
What is outsourcing?
o: Paying another company to do some of your work
qs.why: Outsourcing hands tasks to an outside company.

qs.q: A country imports goods when it sells them to other countries.
qs.why: Selling abroad is exporting; importing means buying from abroad.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of exporting a product in order

lab.q: Challenge: $1 = 0.90 euros. How many euros do you get for $200?
Challenge: A country adds a 10% tariff to a $40 imported item. How many dollars is the tariff?
Challenge: Paying another company, often abroad, to do some of your work is called what?

learn.b: An entrepreneur starts and runs a business and takes on financial risk. Many great businesses begin by solving a real problem. Example: a tutoring app for students who need homework help.
Your target market is the group of people you want to serve. Market research means collecting information about customers and competitors, by talking to people or using surveys.
A value proposition explains why customers should choose you. It answers: what problem do you solve and why are you better? Keep it short and clear.

qs.q: What is an entrepreneur?
o: Someone who only works for others
Someone who starts and runs a business and takes risk
qs.why: Entrepreneurs create businesses and accept financial risk.

qs.q: Good business ideas often do what?
o: Solve a real problem for customers
qs.why: Solving a problem gives people a reason to buy.

qs.q: What is a value proposition?
o: The reason customers should choose your product
qs.why: It states the benefit you offer.

qs.q: What is market research?
o: Collecting information about customers and competitors
qs.why: Research helps you understand the market before you spend.

qs.q: Talking to potential customers before launching can reduce risk.
qs.why: You learn what people want before investing heavily.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of developing an idea in order

lab.q: Challenge: The group of people you want to serve is called your target what? (two words: target ___)
lab.hint: Think of who you aim at.
lab.why: Your target market is the group you aim to serve.

lab.q: Challenge: Collecting information about customers and competitors is called market what?
lab.hint: It is about finding things out.
lab.why: Market research gathers facts about customers and rivals.

lab.q: Challenge: A short statement of why customers should choose you is a value what?
lab.why: A value proposition says what problem you solve and why you are better.

learn.b: Primary research is information you collect yourself, such as surveys and interviews. Secondary research uses data someone else already collected, like reports and articles. Use both to learn about customers and rivals.
Validation means checking that real customers want your idea before you spend a lot. Ask about what people did in the past, not what they might do. Opinions like 'nice idea' are weak proof.

The strongest sign is when people pay or pre-order. A landing page with a sign-up form is a cheap test. Market size can be estimated as number of customers times price, for example 1,000 customers x $20 = $20,000.

qs.q: Which is an example of primary research?
o: A survey you send to customers
qs.why: Primary research is collected by you.

qs.q: What does validating an idea mean?
o: Checking that real customers want it before investing heavily
qs.why: Validation tests demand early.

qs.q: Which is the strongest sign of demand?
o: Friends say it is a nice idea
You feel sure it will work
qs.why: Spending money shows real interest.

qs.q: How does competitor analysis help?
o: It shows how others serve customers and where gaps are
qs.why: You can find what rivals miss.

qs.q: Secondary research uses data someone else already collected.
qs.why: Reports and articles are secondary sources.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Customer pays before it is ready

qs.q: Put the idea validation steps in order

lab.q: Challenge: A market has 2,500 possible customers who would each pay $40. What is the market size in dollars?
Challenge: In a survey of 200 people, 50 say they would buy. What percent is that?
Challenge: Information you collect yourself is called what kind of research?
lab.why: Collecting data yourself is primary research.

learn.b: A business plan is a written plan of your goals and how to reach them. An MVP, minimum viable product, is the simplest version you can test with real customers. It saves time and money.
Startup costs are what you must spend before earning, such as equipment, a website and licenses. Estimate them to know how much money you need.

Bootstrapping uses your own savings and sales. A loan must be repaid with interest but you keep ownership. Equity investors give money for a share of ownership. Crowdfunding collects small sums from many people.

qs.q: What is an MVP?
o: The simplest version you can test with customers
qs.why: An MVP tests the idea with minimal effort.

qs.q: What is bootstrapping?
o: Funding a business with your own savings and sales
qs.why: Bootstrapped founders rely on their own money.

qs.q: What does an equity investor receive?
qs.why: Equity means ownership in the company.

qs.q: What is a business plan?
o: A written plan of goals and how to reach them
qs.why: It lays out the idea, market, costs and goals.

qs.q: A loan gives the lender part ownership of your business.
qs.why: A loan is repaid with interest; it does not give ownership.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the startup steps in order

lab.q: Challenge: What three-letter abbreviation means the simplest version of a product you can test?
lab.why: An MVP lets you test with real customers cheaply.

lab.q: Challenge: Startup costs: equipment $1,500, website $300, license $200. What is the total in dollars?
Challenge: Funding a business with your own savings and sales is called what? (one word ending in -ing)
lab.hint: Pulling yourself up by your bootstraps.

learn.b: A business model is how a company creates value and earns money. A subscription charges customers regularly. Freemium gives a free basic version and charges for upgrades. A marketplace takes a commission, a share of each sale.
Contribution per unit is price minus variable cost. If the price is $20 and the variable cost is $8, each unit contributes $12. Margin percent is that amount divided by price, here 60%.
Cost-plus pricing adds a markup to cost. Value-based pricing uses what customers think the product is worth. Fixed costs, like rent, stay the same as sales change. Variable costs rise with each unit.

qs.q: A monthly payment for a streaming service is an example of a:
qs.why: Customers pay regularly.

qs.q: What does freemium mean?
o: A free basic version with paid upgrades
A product that is always free
A free trial that never ends
qs.why: Freemium mixes free and paid.

qs.q: Price is $20 and variable cost is $8. What is the contribution per unit?
Which cost stays the same when you sell more units?
qs.why: Rent is a fixed cost.

qs.q: Value-based pricing sets the price from what customers think the product is worth.
qs.why: It looks at customer value, not just cost.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Stays the same as sales change

qs.q: Put the steps of cost-plus pricing in order
items: Work out the cost per unit

lab.q: Challenge: A product sells for $25 and costs $10 to make. What is the margin as a percent of price?
Challenge: A product costs $12 and you add a 50% markup. What is the price in dollars?
Challenge: Fixed costs are $900 and each unit contributes $15. How many units to break even?

learn.b: Cost-plus pricing means cost plus a markup. If a product costs $6 and you add a 50% markup, the price is $9. Prices that are too low can cause losses, and too high can scare customers away.
Break-even is when revenue equals costs. If fixed costs are $100 and each sale adds $5 after variable costs, you need 20 sales to break even.
Customer feedback shows what to improve. A pivot is a big change in strategy based on what you learn. Scaling means growing without costs rising as fast as sales.

qs.q: A product costs $6 to make. With a 50% markup on cost, what is the price?
Fixed costs are $100 and each sale adds $5 toward them. How many sales to break even?
What is a pivot?
o: A change in strategy based on what you learn
qs.why: Startups pivot when evidence shows a better path.

qs.q: What does scaling mean?
o: Growing without costs rising as fast as sales
qs.why: Scaling grows revenue faster than costs.

qs.q: A price that is too low can never hurt a business.
qs.why: Very low prices can fail to cover costs and cause losses.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the growth stages in order

lab.q: Challenge: A product costs $8 and you add a 25% markup. What is the price in dollars?
Challenge: Fixed costs are $300 and each sale adds $6 after variable costs. How many sales are needed to break even?
Challenge: What do we call a big change in strategy based on what you learned from customers?
lab.why: A pivot changes direction based on feedback.

learn.b: A lead is a person who might buy. Many leads enter the sales funnel: awareness, interest, decision, action. The action stage is the purchase. Fewer people reach each next step.
A pitch is a short, clear explanation of what you offer. An objection is a reason the customer hesitates, like price. Good sellers listen first and answer the real concern.

Fast, polite service keeps customers coming back. A CRM, customer relationship management tool, stores customer details. Happy customers tell friends, which is word of mouth. Conversion rate is buyers divided by leads.

qs.q: What is a lead?
qs.why: Leads are possible customers.

qs.q: What is the best way to handle a customer complaint?
o: Listen, apologize if needed and fix the problem
qs.why: Solving problems keeps trust.

qs.q: At which funnel stage does the person actually buy?
qs.why: Action is the purchase.

qs.q: What is an objection in sales?
o: A reason a customer hesitates to buy
qs.why: Objections are doubts to answer.

qs.q: Happy customers can bring new customers through word of mouth.
qs.why: People recommend what they like.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the sales funnel stages in order

lab.q: Challenge: Out of 200 leads, 30 bought. What is the conversion rate as a percent?
Challenge: When customers tell their friends about you, it is called word of what?
lab.hint: You use your mouth to speak.
lab.why: Word of mouth spreads by people talking.

lab.q: Challenge: 50 customers each buy a $30 item. What is the revenue in dollars?

learn.b: Good leaders share a clear goal and delegate, which means giving tasks to others. They also listen. Setbacks are normal, and smart founders learn from them.
Intellectual property protects creations. A patent protects an invention. A trademark protects a name or logo. A copyright protects creative works like writing and music.
Ethics means honest ads, fair pay and respecting customers. Trust helps a business grow over time.

qs.q: What does a trademark protect?
qs.why: Trademarks protect identifiers of a brand.

qs.q: What does a patent protect?
qs.why: Patents cover new inventions.

qs.q: What does a copyright protect?
o: Creative works like writing or music
qs.why: Copyright covers original creative works.

qs.q: What does delegation mean?
qs.why: Delegating shares work with team members.

qs.q: A trademark can protect a brand logo.
qs.why: Logos are a classic trademark use.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of learning from a setback in order

lab.q: Challenge: Giving tasks to other people to do is called what?
lab.why: Delegating spreads the work and builds trust.

lab.q: Challenge: Which kind of intellectual property protects an invention?
Challenge: Which kind of intellectual property protects a name or logo?
lab.why: A trademark protects names and logos.

learn.b: Scaling means revenue grows faster than costs. Systems, software and good hiring help. A franchise lets others use your brand and system for fees. The owner is the franchisor and the user is the franchisee.
Growing startups often raise money in stages: seed, Series A, Series B and later. Investors give money for ownership and expect fast growth. More funding means owners keep a smaller share.

An exit is how owners leave or cash out. In an acquisition another company buys the business. In an IPO, initial public offering, shares are first sold to the public. Valuation is the estimated worth of a business, sometimes a multiple of profit.

qs.q: What is scaling?
qs.why: Scaling means efficient growth.

qs.q: What is an IPO?
o: The first sale of company shares to the public
qs.why: IPO means initial public offering.

qs.q: In a franchise, what does the franchisee do?
o: Pays fees to use the franchisor's brand and system
qs.why: The franchisee uses someone else's model.

qs.q: What is an acquisition?
qs.why: The buyer takes over the business.

qs.q: Scaling just means spending as much money as possible.
qs.why: Scaling is about growing without costs rising as fast.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: License to use a brand and system

qs.q: Put these funding stages in a typical order

lab.q: Challenge: A business earns $40,000 profit and is valued at 5 times profit. What is the valuation in dollars?
Challenge: A franchisee pays 5% of $80,000 in sales as a fee. How many dollars is the fee?
Challenge: What three-letter term means a company first sells its shares to the public?

learn.b: Marketing is everything a business does to understand customers and get them interested in its products. Advertising is only one part.
The 4 Ps are Product (what you sell), Price (what it costs), Place (where it is sold) and Promotion (how you tell people). Together they form a marketing mix.
No product suits everyone. A target market is the group you aim at. Segmentation divides people by age, interests or needs so you can speak to them directly.

qs.q: Which are the 4 Ps of marketing?
qs.why: The marketing mix is product, price, place and promotion.

qs.q: Which P describes where a product is sold?
qs.why: Place covers where and how customers can buy.

qs.q: What is a target market?
o: The group of customers a business aims at
qs.why: Businesses focus on the people most likely to buy.

qs.q: What is segmentation?
o: Dividing a market into groups with similar traits
qs.why: Segments help tailor messages to groups.

qs.q: Marketing means only advertising.
qs.why: Marketing also includes research, pricing, product design and distribution.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the marketing planning steps in order

lab.q: Challenge: Which of the 4 Ps describes where a product is sold?
lab.hint: Starts with P and is about location.
lab.why: Place covers where and how customers can buy.

lab.q: Challenge: Which of the 4 Ps is about what a product costs?
lab.why: Price is the amount customers pay.

lab.q: Challenge: The group of people a business aims at is called its target what?
lab.hint: Not 'audience' here: think of a place to buy and sell.
lab.why: The target market is the group the business aims at.

learn.b: Buyers usually go through steps: they notice a need, search for information, compare options, buy, and then feel good or bad about it. That last feeling affects whether they buy again.
Personal factors are needs and taste. Social factors are friends, family and trends. Psychological factors are perception and motivation. Price and quality matter too.
Qualitative research collects opinions and reasons, for example interviews and focus groups. Quantitative research collects numbers from many people, like a large survey. Marketers often use both.

qs.q: What is the first step in the buying process?
qs.why: Buying starts when you notice a need.

qs.q: What is a focus group?
o: A small group that discusses a product with a researcher
qs.why: It is a form of qualitative research.

qs.q: Quantitative research gives you:
qs.why: Quantitative means measurable numbers.

qs.q: Friends and trends are an example of which influence?
qs.why: Other people shape what we buy.

qs.q: How customers feel after buying matters because it affects repeat purchases.
qs.why: Happy buyers return.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the buying process in order

lab.q: Challenge: In a survey of 1,200 people, 300 prefer red. What percent is that?
Challenge: A survey asks 2,000 people to rate a product from 1 to 5. Is it qualitative or quantitative research?
lab.why: Ratings give numbers, so it is quantitative.

lab.q: Challenge: The first step in buying is recognizing a what?

learn.b: A brand is the identity and feeling people connect with a business. It includes the name, logo, colors and promises. A strong brand is easy to remember.
A USP, unique selling proposition, is what makes you different from others. Positioning is the place your brand holds in customers' minds compared with competitors.
Brand voice is the personality in your words, like friendly or serious. Using the same voice and look everywhere builds trust and recognition.

qs.q: What is a brand?
o: The identity and feeling people connect with a business
qs.why: A brand is more than a logo; it is the whole impression.

qs.q: What does USP stand for?
qs.why: A USP is what makes you different.

qs.q: What is positioning?
o: Your brand's place in customers' minds versus rivals
qs.why: Positioning is about perception relative to competitors.

qs.q: What is brand voice?
o: The personality of a brand's words
qs.why: Voice shows personality in how a brand communicates.

qs.q: Consistent branding helps customers recognize a business.
qs.why: Repetition builds familiarity and trust.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of building a brand in order

lab.q: Challenge: What does USP stand for? (three words)
Challenge: The personality in a brand's words, like friendly or serious, is its brand what?
lab.hint: You hear it in how it speaks.
lab.why: Brand voice is the personality in the words.

lab.q: Challenge: The place a brand holds in customers' minds compared with competitors is called what?
lab.why: Positioning is the brand's place in customers' minds.

learn.b: Segmentation divides a market into groups. Demographic uses age, income or gender. Geographic uses location. Psychographic uses lifestyle and values. Behavioral uses how people buy or use a product.
Targeting is choosing which segments to serve. A niche market is a small, specific segment, like vegan hiking snacks. Focusing lets a small business compete with big ones.

Positioning is the image you want in the target's mind. Marketers write a short positioning statement and then design the marketing mix to match it. The steps are Segment, Target, Position, often called STP.

qs.q: Dividing customers by age and income is which kind of segmentation?
qs.why: Age and income are demographics.

qs.q: Dividing customers by city or climate is which kind of segmentation?
qs.why: Location-based.

qs.q: What does the T in STP stand for?
qs.why: Segment, Target, Position.

qs.q: What is a niche market?
qs.why: Niches are narrow groups.

qs.q: Psychographic segmentation uses lifestyle and values.
qs.why: It looks at attitudes and interests.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the STP process in order

lab.q: Challenge: Segmenting customers by where they live is called what kind of segmentation?
Challenge: A market has 5,000 teens and you expect to reach 10% of them. How many teens is that?
Challenge: What does the S in STP stand for?

learn.b: Penetration pricing starts low to win customers quickly. Price skimming starts high and lowers the price later. Psychological pricing, like $9.99 instead of $10, makes prices feel smaller. Competitive pricing follows rivals.
The promotion mix has advertising (paid messages), sales promotion (coupons, discounts), public relations (news and events) and personal selling. Using them together works best.
A discount lowers the price by a percent. To find 20% off $50, take 20% of 50, which is $10, and subtract: $40. Always check that a sale price still covers your costs.

qs.q: What is penetration pricing?
o: Starting low to win customers quickly
qs.why: The low price helps enter the market.

qs.q: What is price skimming?
o: A high price at first, lowered later
qs.why: Early buyers pay more.

qs.q: Pricing a product at $9.99 instead of $10 is an example of:
qs.why: The price looks smaller.

qs.q: A coupon is an example of:
qs.why: Coupons give a short-term incentive.

qs.q: Public relations tries to build a good image through news and events, not paid ads.
qs.why: PR earns attention rather than buying it.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Image built through news and events

qs.q: Put the steps of a promotion campaign in order

lab.q: Challenge: A $60 jacket is 20% off. What is the sale price in dollars?
Challenge: A product costs $15 to make and you add a 40% markup. What is the price in dollars?
Challenge: Pricing low to enter a market and win customers is called what kind of pricing?

learn.b: SEO, search engine optimization, means improving your website so it shows higher in search results without paying for ads. Content marketing means sharing useful posts or videos to attract customers.
Social media lets brands talk with people directly. Email reaches people who already signed up. A CTA, call to action, tells people what to do next, like Sign up now.
A conversion happens when a visitor does what you wanted, such as buying. CTR, click-through rate, is the percent of viewers who click. If 1,000 people see an ad and 50 click, CTR is 5%.

qs.q: What does SEO try to do?
o: Help a website rank higher in search results
qs.why: SEO improves organic visibility.

qs.q: What is a CTA?
o: A prompt telling people what to do next
qs.why: CTA means call to action.

qs.q: An ad is seen 1,000 times and clicked 50 times. What is the CTR?
What is a conversion?
o: A visitor taking the desired action
qs.why: A conversion is a completed goal like a purchase or sign-up.

qs.q: SEO means paying for search ads.
qs.why: SEO is about earning higher results unpaid, not buying ads.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the customer journey in order

lab.q: Challenge: An ad is seen 2,000 times and clicked 100 times. What is the CTR as a percent?
Challenge: What does SEO stand for? (three words)
lab.hint: It helps you show up in search.

lab.q: Challenge: CTA stands for call to what?
lab.hint: A CTA tells people what to do.

learn.b: Impressions count how many times an ad was shown. Conversion rate is conversions divided by visitors. If 500 visitors lead to 25 buyers, the conversion rate is 5%.
ROI, return on investment, is (gain - cost) / cost x 100. If an ad costs $200 and brings $500 in revenue, ROI is (500 - 200) / 200 = 150%. A positive ROI means the campaign earned more than it cost.

CAC is the cost to win one new customer. CLV, customer lifetime value, is the total a customer brings over time. A healthy business has CLV higher than CAC. Dashboards show these numbers in one place.

qs.q: Conversion rate is calculated as:
qs.why: It shows what share of visitors take action.

qs.q: An ad costs $400 and brings $1,000 in revenue. What is ROI using (revenue - cost) / cost?
What does CAC mean?
o: The cost to win one new customer
qs.why: Customer acquisition cost.

qs.q: For a healthy business, CLV should be:
qs.why: A customer should bring more than they cost to win.

qs.q: Impressions count how many times an ad was shown.
qs.why: One showing equals one impression.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Total value of a customer over time

qs.q: Put the analytics cycle in order

lab.q: Challenge: 500 visitors lead to 25 purchases. What is the conversion rate as a percent?
Challenge: An ad costs $200 and brings $500 in revenue. What is the ROI as a percent using (revenue - cost) / cost?
lab.hint: Subtract first, then divide by cost.

lab.q: Challenge: A customer spends $30 per order, 4 times a year, for 3 years. What is the customer lifetime value in dollars?

learn.b: A survey asks people for opinions. An A/B test shows two versions, like two ad headlines, to different groups and compares which works better.
Retention means keeping existing customers buying. Customer acquisition cost is how much it costs to win a new customer. Keeping a customer is often cheaper than finding a new one.
Ads should not make false claims. Misleading customers can break the law and harms trust. Ethical marketing respects privacy and tells the truth.

qs.q: What is an A/B test?
o: Comparing two versions to see which performs better
qs.why: A/B tests compare two options with real audiences.

qs.q: What is customer retention?
qs.why: Retention is about repeat business.

qs.q: What is a survey?
qs.why: Surveys gather customer feedback.

qs.q: Why is false advertising a problem?
o: It is unethical and can be illegal
qs.why: Misleading claims harm customers and break trust.

qs.q: Keeping an existing customer is often cheaper than winning a new one.
qs.why: New customers usually require more marketing spend.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Cost to win a new customer

qs.q: Put the steps of an A/B test in order

lab.q: Challenge: Showing two versions of an ad to different groups to see which works better is an A/B what?
Challenge: Keeping existing customers buying is called what?
Challenge: You spend $500 on ads and win 25 new customers. What is the cost per new customer in dollars?

learn.b: Accounting records, summarizes and reports a business's money. Bookkeeping is the day-to-day recording of transactions. Owners, banks and tax offices use the reports.
Assets are things the business owns, like cash and equipment. Liabilities are what it owes, like loans. Equity is the owner's share after debts are paid.
Assets = Liabilities + Equity. This always balances. If assets are $500 and liabilities are $200, equity is $300.

qs.q: What is the accounting equation?
qs.why: The two sides of the balance sheet must always match.

qs.q: Which is an asset?
qs.why: Assets are resources owned by the business.

qs.q: Which is a liability?
qs.why: Liabilities are amounts the business owes.

qs.q: What is bookkeeping?
qs.why: Bookkeepers keep daily financial records.

qs.q: If assets are $500 and liabilities are $200, equity is $300.
Match each term to its meaning
Put the basic accounting steps in order

lab.q: Challenge: Assets are $800 and liabilities are $300. What is equity in dollars?
Challenge: Assets are $1,000 and equity is $400. What are liabilities in dollars?
Challenge: What is the day-to-day recording of transactions called?

learn.b: In double-entry bookkeeping, every transaction affects at least two accounts. Total debits always equal total credits. This helps catch mistakes.
A debit is an entry on the left side of an account. A credit is on the right. Debits increase assets and expenses. Credits increase liabilities, equity and revenue.
The journal records transactions in date order. The ledger groups them by account. If you pay cash for equipment, equipment goes up and cash goes down.

qs.q: What does double-entry mean?
o: Every transaction is recorded twice in different books only
Every transaction affects at least two accounts
qs.why: Each transaction has a debit side and a credit side.

qs.q: Which side increases an asset account?
qs.why: Debits increase asset accounts.

qs.q: A business pays cash for new equipment. What changes?
o: Equipment goes up and cash goes down
qs.why: One asset rises while another asset falls.

qs.q: What is a ledger?
qs.why: The ledger organizes transactions by account.

qs.q: A debit always means a decrease.
qs.why: Debits increase assets and expenses, and decrease liabilities.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the recording steps in order

lab.q: Challenge: In double-___ bookkeeping, every transaction affects at least two accounts. What word fills the blank?
lab.why: Double-entry means two sides for each transaction.

lab.q: Challenge: Debits increase assets and which other kind of account?
Challenge: The journal records transactions in what order?
lab.why: The journal lists transactions in order by date.

learn.b: At the end of a period, accountants adjust the books so revenue and expenses match the period they belong to. This follows accrual accounting. Adjusting entries are made before preparing financial statements.

An accrued expense is incurred but not yet paid, like wages owed: debit expense, credit liability. A prepaid expense is paid in advance, like $1,200 of insurance for 12 months, so $100 becomes expense each month. Unearned revenue is cash received before the work is done. It is a liability.

Straight-line depreciation spreads cost evenly: (cost - salvage value) / useful life. Salvage value is the estimated value at the end. A $10,000 asset with $1,000 salvage and 3 years of life loses $3,000 per year.

qs.q: Wages earned by workers but not yet paid are an example of:
qs.why: They are incurred but unpaid.

qs.q: A customer pays $600 in advance for six months of service. Before the service is given, the money is:
o: An asset you own for free
qs.why: You owe the service, so it is a liability.

qs.q: Prepaid insurance is recorded as:
o: An asset until it is used up
qs.why: It has future value to the business.

qs.q: Cost $10,000, salvage $1,000, life 3 years. What is the yearly straight-line depreciation?
Adjusting entries are made at the end of a period so the records match accrual accounting.
qs.why: They place revenue and expenses in the right period.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Cash received before work is done
Estimated value at end of life

qs.q: Put these steps in order

lab.q: Challenge: A business prepays $2,400 of rent for 12 months. How many dollars of rent expense per month?
Challenge: A machine costs $5,000, has $500 salvage value and lasts 5 years. What is the yearly straight-line depreciation in dollars?
Challenge: Cash received before the work is done is called what kind of revenue?
lab.why: It is unearned revenue until the work is done.

units.title: Inventory and Cost of Goods Sold

learn.b: Inventory is goods held for sale. It is a current asset on the balance sheet. When goods are sold, their cost moves to an expense called cost of goods sold (COGS).
COGS = beginning inventory + purchases - ending inventory. If you start with $2,000, buy $6,000 and end with $1,500, COGS is $6,500. Gross profit is sales minus COGS.

FIFO means first in, first out: the oldest items are assumed sold first. LIFO means last in, first out. Weighted average uses the average cost. When prices rise, FIFO usually gives a lower COGS and a higher profit than LIFO.

qs.q: What does FIFO mean?
o: The last items bought are sold first
The first items bought are assumed sold first
qs.why: First in, first out.

qs.q: Beginning inventory $2,000, purchases $6,000, ending inventory $1,500. What is COGS?
When prices are rising, which method usually gives the lower COGS?
qs.why: Older, cheaper costs go to COGS under FIFO.

qs.q: Where does inventory appear?
o: As an asset on the balance sheet
qs.why: It is something the business owns.

qs.q: Cost of goods sold is the cost of items a business actually sold in the period.
qs.why: Unsold goods stay in inventory.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps to find COGS in order

lab.q: Challenge: Beginning inventory is $3,000, purchases are $8,000 and ending inventory is $2,500. What is COGS in dollars?
Challenge: You buy 10 units at $2 and then 10 units at $3. Using FIFO, what is the COGS in dollars of selling 10 units?
lab.hint: The oldest units are sold first.
lab.why: The first 10 units cost $2 each: 10 x 2 = 20.

lab.q: Challenge: Sales are $15,000 and COGS is $9,000. What is the gross profit in dollars?

learn.b: The income statement shows revenue, expenses and profit over a period, like a month. Net income = revenue - expenses. Example: $500 revenue and $350 expenses leaves $150.
The balance sheet is a snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity on one date. It shows what the business owns and owes at that moment.
The cash flow statement shows cash coming in and going out. A business can show profit but still lack cash. Owners check all three statements.

qs.q: What does an income statement show?
o: Revenue, expenses and profit over a period
qs.why: It covers performance across a period.

qs.q: What does a balance sheet show?
o: Assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time
qs.why: It is a snapshot at a specific date.

qs.q: Revenue is $500 and expenses are $350. What is net income?
What does a cash flow statement show?
o: Cash coming in and going out
qs.why: It tracks cash movements.

qs.q: A balance sheet is a snapshot at one date.
qs.why: It reports balances at a specific point in time.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Snapshot of what is owned and owed

qs.q: Put these income statement lines in order from top to bottom

lab.q: Challenge: Revenue is $2,000 and expenses are $1,350. What is net income in dollars?
Challenge: Which statement is a snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity on one date?
lab.why: The balance sheet is a snapshot.

lab.q: Challenge: Which statement shows cash coming in and going out?
lab.why: The cash flow statement tracks cash movement.

learn.b: The cash flow statement has three sections. Operating is day-to-day sales and expenses. Investing is buying or selling long-term assets like equipment. Financing is loans, owner money and dividends.

Working capital = current assets - current liabilities. It shows if a business can pay its short-term bills. Accounts receivable is money customers owe the business. Accounts payable is money the business owes suppliers.
A business can show a profit but run out of cash if customers pay late or if it spends heavily on inventory. Owners watch cash closely. Net change in cash is operating + investing + financing.

qs.q: Buying new equipment appears in which section?
qs.why: Long-term assets are investing.

qs.q: Taking out a bank loan appears in which section?
qs.why: Loans and owner funds are financing.

qs.q: What is working capital?
qs.why: It measures short-term strength.

qs.q: What are accounts receivable?
qs.why: Receivable means to be received.

qs.q: A profitable company can still run short of cash when customers pay slowly.
qs.why: Profit is not the same as cash in hand.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the cash flow statement sections in their usual order

lab.q: Challenge: Current assets are $12,000 and current liabilities are $7,500. What is working capital in dollars?
Challenge: Operating cash flow is +$5,000, investing is -$3,000 and financing is +$1,000. What is the net change in cash in dollars?
Challenge: Money a business owes to suppliers is called accounts what?
lab.why: Accounts payable are bills still to pay.

learn.b: Gross profit = revenue - cost of goods sold. The current ratio = current assets / current liabilities. If you have $200 of current assets and $100 of current liabilities, it is 2.
Depreciation spreads the cost of an asset, like a machine, over its useful life. A $1,000 machine lasting 5 years can be recorded as $200 of expense per year.
Accrual accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, even if cash moves later. Cash-basis records when cash moves. An audit is an independent check of financial records.

qs.q: How is gross profit calculated?
o: Revenue minus cost of goods sold
qs.why: Gross profit is sales minus direct production cost.

qs.q: Current assets are $200 and current liabilities are $100. What is the current ratio?
What does depreciation do?
o: Spreads an asset's cost over its useful life
qs.why: It matches an asset's cost to the years it is used.

qs.q: When does accrual accounting record revenue?
qs.why: Accrual records revenue when earned, not when paid.

qs.q: Under cash-basis accounting, revenue is recorded when the sale is made even if unpaid.
qs.why: Cash-basis records revenue when cash is actually received.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put these profit lines in order from top to bottom

lab.q: Challenge: Revenue is $900 and cost of goods sold is $550. What is gross profit in dollars?
Challenge: Current assets are $300 and current liabilities are $150. What is the current ratio?
Challenge: A $6,000 machine lasts 10 years with no leftover value. How many dollars of depreciation per year?

learn.b: Financial accounting reports to outsiders like banks and investors. Managerial accounting helps managers inside the business make decisions. It does not have to follow the same strict reporting rules.
A budget is a plan of expected income and spending. A variance is actual minus budget. If you planned to spend $1,000 and spent $1,200, that is a $200 unfavorable variance.

Fixed costs stay the same, variable costs change with output. Contribution margin = price - variable cost per unit. Break-even units = fixed costs / contribution margin. With fixed costs $6,000, price $20 and variable cost $8, break-even is 6,000 / 12 = 500 units.

qs.q: Who is managerial accounting mainly for?
qs.why: It supports internal decisions.

qs.q: What is a budget?
o: A plan of expected income and spending
qs.why: Budgets look ahead.

qs.q: Fixed costs $6,000, price $20, variable cost $8. What is the break-even in units?
A business budgeted $1,000 but spent $1,200. This is a:
qs.why: Spending went over the plan.

qs.q: A variable cost changes when production changes.
qs.why: More units usually means more materials.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Stays the same as output changes

qs.q: Put the budgeting steps in order
items: Compare actual results with the budget

lab.q: Challenge: Fixed costs are $4,500, price is $15 and variable cost is $6 per unit. How many units to break even?
Challenge: A budget was $800 and actual spending was $950. By how many dollars did spending go over?
Challenge: Price is $40 and variable cost is $25 per unit. What is the contribution margin per unit in dollars?

learn.b: Residential property is for living, like houses and apartments. Commercial property is for business, like offices and shops. Land can be used for either or kept as it is.
Renters pay a landlord and do not build ownership. Owners pay for upkeep, taxes and often a mortgage, but build equity. Equity is the home's value minus the loan still owed.
Appreciation is when a property's value rises over time. Values can also fall. Location, demand and the economy all matter.

qs.q: What is residential property?
o: Property meant for people to live in
qs.why: Residential means homes where people live.

qs.q: How is home equity calculated?
qs.why: Equity is your ownership share after the loan.

qs.q: What is appreciation?
o: A rise in a property's value
qs.why: Appreciation means value goes up over time.

qs.q: Who does a renter pay?
qs.why: Rent is paid to the property owner or landlord.

qs.q: Renting a home builds ownership equity.
qs.why: Rent payments do not give the renter ownership of the property.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of renting a home in order

lab.q: Challenge: A home is worth $250,000 and the loan owed is $180,000. What is the equity in dollars?
Challenge: A $200,000 property rises 5% in value. What is its new value in dollars?
Challenge: Property made for people to live in, like houses and apartments, is what kind of property?

learn.b: A mortgage is a loan used to buy property. The property is collateral. If payments stop, the lender can take the property in a process called foreclosure.
A down payment is the part of the price you pay up front in cash. On a $200,000 home, a 10% down payment is $20,000. The rest is borrowed. Principal is the amount borrowed.
A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same interest rate for its whole term. An adjustable-rate mortgage can change over time. Amortization is paying off the loan gradually through regular payments.

qs.q: What is a down payment?
o: Money paid up front toward the price
qs.why: It is the cash you pay at the start of the purchase.

qs.q: A home costs $200,000. How much is a 10% down payment?
What does a fixed-rate mortgage mean?
o: The price of the house is fixed
The interest rate stays the same for the term
qs.why: A fixed rate does not change over the term.

qs.q: What secures a mortgage loan?
qs.why: The home acts as collateral for the lender.

qs.q: If you stop paying a mortgage, the lender may take the property through foreclosure.
qs.why: Foreclosure lets the lender recover money by taking the property.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the path to buying with a mortgage in order

lab.q: Challenge: A 20% down payment on a $300,000 home is how many dollars?
Challenge: A home costs $250,000 and you pay 10% down. How many dollars do you borrow?
Challenge: What is it called when a lender takes a property after payments stop?

learn.b: Market value is the price a willing buyer would reasonably pay a willing seller. It is not the same as the asking price, which is the listing price. The assessed value is the value used for property tax.

Appraisers use comparables, or comps: similar nearby properties sold recently. They adjust for differences like size and condition. Price per square foot is price divided by area, for example $300,000 / 1,500 sq ft = $200.
Location matters most: schools, jobs and safety. Size, age, condition and upgrades also matter. A lender orders an appraisal so it does not lend more than the property is worth.

qs.q: What are comps?
o: Similar nearby properties that sold recently
qs.why: Comparables guide the value.

qs.q: A 1,500 sq ft home sells for $300,000. What is the price per square foot?
Which factor usually affects value the most?
qs.why: Location drives demand.

qs.q: Who usually orders an appraisal?
qs.why: The lender protects its loan.

qs.q: Market value is what a willing buyer would reasonably pay a willing seller.
qs.why: That is the standard definition.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the appraisal steps in order

lab.q: Challenge: A home has 2,000 sq ft and similar homes sell for $175 per sq ft. What is the estimated value in dollars?
lab.hint: Multiply area by price per sq ft.

lab.q: Challenge: Comps average $210 per sq ft. A home has 1,200 sq ft. What is its estimated value in dollars?
Challenge: Similar nearby properties that sold recently, used to estimate value, are called what? (one word, plural)

learn.b: A sale is made by a written contract, called a purchase agreement. Contingencies are conditions, like a good inspection or loan approval, that let the buyer cancel if they are not met. Earnest money is a deposit showing the buyer is serious.

Title means the legal right to own a property. A title search checks the ownership history and any liens, which are legal claims for unpaid debts. Title insurance protects against hidden ownership problems.
At closing, the buyer signs loan papers, pays the remaining money and closing costs, and receives the deed. The deed is the document that transfers ownership. Then the buyer gets the keys.

qs.q: What does a deed do?
o: It transfers ownership of the property
qs.why: The deed shows who owns the property.

qs.q: What is a contingency?
o: A condition that must be met or the buyer can cancel
qs.why: Example: loan approval.

qs.q: What does a title search check?
qs.why: It looks for claims against the property.

qs.q: What is earnest money?
o: A deposit showing the buyer is serious
qs.why: It is paid early with the offer.

qs.q: A real estate sales contract should be in writing.
qs.why: Verbal agreements are generally not enough for property sales.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Final meeting to complete the sale

qs.q: Put the buying steps in order
items: Seller accepts and the contract is signed

lab.q: Challenge: Earnest money is 1% of a $250,000 price. How many dollars is the deposit?
Challenge: A legal claim against a property for an unpaid debt is called a what?
Challenge: What document transfers ownership of a property?

learn.b: An inspection checks the condition of the home. An appraisal estimates its market value, and lenders use it to decide how much they will lend.
Closing costs are fees paid when the sale is finished. Owners also pay property tax to local government, homeowner insurance and maintenance. These are on top of the mortgage.
Escrow is when a neutral third party holds money or documents until all conditions of the deal are met. Many lenders also collect taxes and insurance through an escrow account.

qs.q: What does a home inspection do?
o: Examines the condition of the home
qs.why: Inspectors look for problems in the building.

qs.q: What is an appraisal?
o: An estimate of a property's value
qs.why: Appraisers estimate market value.

qs.q: What are closing costs?
o: The cost of closing a bank account
Fees paid when the purchase is completed
qs.why: They cover loan, legal and other fees at closing.

qs.q: Who receives property tax?
qs.why: Property tax funds local services.

qs.q: An appraisal is a monthly loan payment.
qs.why: An appraisal is an estimate of value, not a payment.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the buying steps in order

lab.q: Challenge: What do we call a neutral third party holding money until a deal's conditions are met?
lab.why: Escrow holds funds for both sides.

lab.q: Challenge: Which check estimates a home's market value for the lender?
Challenge: Yearly property tax is $2,400 and yearly insurance is $1,200. How many dollars per month go into escrow for both?

learn.b: A lease is a written agreement between a landlord (owner) and a tenant (renter). It states the rent, length, rules and who pays for what. A security deposit is money held to cover damage or unpaid rent.
The landlord must keep the home safe and livable. The tenant must pay rent on time and take care of the home. Evictions must follow legal steps. A landlord cannot simply change the locks.
A common guideline is that rent should be about 30% of gross income or less. If you earn $4,000 per month, 30% is $1,200. Check the total yearly cost too: monthly rent times 12.

qs.q: What is a security deposit?
o: Money held to cover damage or unpaid rent
The first month of rent only
qs.why: It is returned if nothing is wrong.

qs.q: What is a lease?
o: A written agreement between landlord and tenant
qs.why: It sets the rules of the rental.

qs.q: A common guideline says rent should be no more than about what share of gross income?
qs.why: The 30% rule is a rough guide.

qs.q: Who normally must keep a rental safe and livable?
qs.why: Landlords must maintain habitable homes.

qs.q: A landlord can usually remove a tenant by changing the locks without any legal process.
qs.why: Evictions must follow the legal process.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Legal process to remove a tenant

qs.q: Put the renting steps in order
items: Apply and pass a credit check
Sign the lease and pay the deposit
Move in and note any damage

lab.q: Challenge: Your income is $4,000 per month. How many dollars is 30% of it for rent?
Challenge: Rent is $900 per month on a 12-month lease. What is the total rent for the lease in dollars?
Challenge: A $1,000 deposit has $250 deducted for damage. How many dollars are returned?

learn.b: Local governments charge property tax based on assessed value times a tax rate. A home assessed at $200,000 with a 1.2% rate pays $2,400 per year. It is paid every year, even after the mortgage is paid off.

Homeowners insurance covers damage like fire and theft. It usually does not cover floods, which need separate flood insurance. If your down payment is under 20%, lenders often require PMI, private mortgage insurance, to protect themselves.

A capital gain is profit from selling for more than you paid. Some places tax it, sometimes with a break for a main home. An HOA fee is a regular payment to a homeowners association for shared spaces.

qs.q: PMI is usually required when:
o: The down payment is less than 20%
qs.why: It protects the lender.

qs.q: Standard homeowners insurance usually does not cover:
qs.why: Floods need separate coverage.

qs.q: Property tax is based on:
qs.why: Assessed value times the tax rate.

qs.q: What is a capital gain?
o: Profit from selling an asset for more than you paid
qs.why: Sale price minus purchase price.

qs.q: Homeowners insurance can protect against fire damage.
qs.why: Fire is a standard covered risk.

learn.b: Owners can rent property to earn income. Cash flow from a rental is rent minus costs such as the mortgage, taxes, insurance and repairs. Vacancy, when no one is renting, means lost income.
Leverage means using borrowed money to buy an asset. It can magnify gains, but it also magnifies losses. Debt still must be repaid if the property falls in value.
A REIT is a company that owns income-producing real estate, and you can buy its shares like a stock. Real estate is illiquid, meaning it can take time to sell and turn into cash.

qs.q: What is a REIT?
o: A company that owns income-producing real estate with shares you can buy
qs.why: REITs let people invest in real estate through shares.

qs.q: How is rental cash flow calculated?
qs.why: Cash flow is income left after costs.

o: Easy to sell in a second
Slow and harder to turn into cash
qs.why: Real estate can take weeks or months to sell.

qs.q: What is vacancy?
o: A period when a unit is empty and earns no rent
qs.why: Empty units do not produce rental income.

qs.q: Using borrowed money to buy property is called leverage and can magnify both gains and losses.
qs.why: Debt amplifies results in both directions.

learn.b: A computer takes input (like typing), processes it, and gives output (like text on the screen). It can also store data for later.
Hardware is the parts you can touch, like the screen and keyboard. Software is the programs and apps that tell the hardware what to do.
Computers use only 0s and 1s. One 0 or 1 is a bit. Eight bits make one byte, which can store one letter like A.

qs.why: A keyboard sends data into the computer, so it is an input device.

qs.q: Which one is software?
qs.why: A web browser is a program, and programs are software.

qs.why: One byte is made of 8 bits.

qs.q: Which digits do computers use to store all data?
qs.why: Computers use the binary system, which has only 0 and 1.

qs.q: A monitor is an output device.
qs.why: A monitor shows information coming out of the computer.

learn.b: The operating system (OS) is the main software of a computer. It manages the hardware and lets apps run. Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS are operating systems.
A file holds data, like a photo or a document. Folders keep files organized. The file extension, like .jpg or .txt, shows the file type.
Save your work often so you do not lose it. A backup is an extra copy of your files in another place, in case something breaks.

qs.q: What is the main job of an operating system?
qs.why: The OS manages the computer's parts and lets programs run.

qs.q: What is a backup?
o: An extra copy of your files
qs.why: A backup is a copy kept safe in case the original is lost.

qs.q: Folders help you organize files.
qs.why: Folders group related files together so they are easy to find.

learn.b: The CPU (central processing unit) runs instructions and does calculations. A faster CPU can do more work each second.
RAM is short-term memory. It holds what you are using now and is erased when the power is off. Storage (SSD or hard drive) keeps files even when the computer is off.
The motherboard connects all the parts together. The GPU handles graphics. The power supply gives the parts electricity.

qs.q: Which part is called the brain of the computer?
qs.why: The CPU runs instructions and does the calculations.

qs.q: What happens to data in RAM when the computer is turned off?
qs.why: RAM is temporary memory and loses its data without power.

qs.q: Which part connects all the main components together?
qs.why: The motherboard is the main circuit board that links the parts.

qs.q: Which part is mainly responsible for graphics?
qs.why: The GPU (graphics processing unit) draws images and video.

qs.q: An SSD keeps your files when the computer is turned off.
qs.why: An SSD is permanent storage, so data stays without power.

learn.b: Computers use binary, which has only 0 and 1. Place values go 8, 4, 2, 1 from the right. So 101 means 4 + 0 + 1 = 5, and 1010 means 8 + 2 = 10.
A bit is one 0 or 1. A byte is 8 bits. A kilobyte (KB) is about a thousand bytes, a megabyte (MB) about a million and a gigabyte (GB) about a billion. A GB is much larger than an MB.

Text is stored using codes that give each character a number, such as ASCII and Unicode. Pictures are made of pixels, tiny dots of color. Each pixel's color is stored as numbers, often red, green and blue.

qs.why: Images are grids of pixels.

qs.why: Byte, KB, MB, GB grow in that order.

qs.q: What do ASCII and Unicode do?

qs.why: Computers store text as numbers.

qs.why: Binary is base 2.

learn.b: A network connects computers so they can share data. A LAN, local area network, covers a small place like a home or school. A WAN covers a large area. The internet is a huge network of networks.

A router sends data between devices and networks. Wi-Fi connects devices without cables. Every device has an IP address. DNS turns names like example.com into IP addresses. Data travels in small pieces called packets.
The web is the websites you open with a browser. The internet is the whole system that carries the web, email and more. An ISP, internet service provider, is the company that gives you access.

qs.q: What does DNS do?
o: Turns website names into IP addresses
qs.why: DNS is like a phone book for the internet.

qs.q: What does a router do?
o: Directs data between devices and networks
qs.why: It sends packets to the right place.

qs.q: What is a packet?
o: A small piece of data sent across a network
qs.why: Data is split into packets.

qs.q: What does a LAN cover?
o: A small area like a home or school
qs.why: LAN means local area network.

qs.q: The web and the internet are exactly the same thing.
qs.why: The web is one service that runs on the internet.

learn.b: System software, like an operating system, runs the computer. Application software, like a word processor or game, does tasks for you. A web browser is an app that opens websites.
Open-source software has code anyone can read and often change. Proprietary software keeps its code private. A license says how you may use the software.

The cloud means storing files or running programs on remote servers over the internet. You can reach your files from many devices and they are backed up. The main downside is that you usually need an internet connection.

qs.why: No internet often means no access.

qs.why: It manages the hardware and runs apps.

learn.b: A strong password is long, unique and hard to guess, like several random words with numbers. Never reuse passwords. A password manager stores them safely. Two-factor authentication (2FA) adds a second proof, such as a code sent to your phone.

Phishing is a fake message that tricks you into giving information. Malware is harmful software, such as viruses and ransomware. Ransomware locks your files and demands money. Do not click unknown links or open strange attachments.
Keep your system updated and use antivirus. A firewall blocks unwanted network traffic. Look for HTTPS and the padlock on websites. Share as little personal information as you can.

qs.q: What is phishing?
o: A fake message that tricks you into giving information
qs.why: Phishers try to steal passwords.

qs.q: Which password is the strongest?
qs.why: Long, mixed and unique.

qs.q: What does two-factor authentication add?
o: A second proof, like a code sent to your phone
qs.why: It protects you if a password leaks.

qs.q: What does ransomware do?
o: Locks your files and demands money
qs.why: It holds your data hostage.

qs.q: You should use the same password for every account.
qs.why: If one account leaks, all of them are at risk.

learn.b: Shortcuts save time. Ctrl+C copies, Ctrl+V pastes, and Ctrl+Z undoes your last action. On a Mac, use Command instead of Ctrl.
Apps are programs for a task, like writing or drawing. Updates fix bugs and add features, so install them when your computer asks.
If a computer is frozen or acting strange, restarting it often helps. Also check cables, close extra programs, and save your work often.
